meta.title: Who really said "The intention of the Holy Ghost is to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Galileo wrote it down — but as a quotation. His own marginal note credits Cardinal Cesare Baronio, who died before the Copernican fight began.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The intention of the Holy Ghost is to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes'?
meta.ogDescription: Galileo introduces the line as something “heard from an ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree.” His marginal note names the man: Cardinal Baronio.

answer.label: Not Galileo — actually Cardinal Cesare Baronio
answer.authorDates: 1538–1607 · Italian cardinal and ecclesiastical historian, of St Philip Neri’s Oratory
answer.sourceLine: The sentence really is in Galileo’s hand — in his Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of 1615 — but he presents it as a quotation, not a coinage. He introduces it as something “heard from an ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree,” and the marginal note printed beside it in the Edizione Nazionale reads simply “Cardinal Baronio” ↗. Baronio died in 1607, eight years before the letter.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina
Cardinal Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), by Galileo’s own marginal note
Stillman Drake’s translation, Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo (1957), p. 186

source.excerpt: Can the Holy Ghost be asserted not to have intended teaching us something that does concern our salvation? I would say here something that was heard from an ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree: “That the intention of the Holy Ghost is to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes.”
trail: Wikiquote carries the line in its sourced section ↗, under the Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615), and prints the bracketed gloss “[probably Caesar Baronius]” against the unnamed ecclesiastic. So even the specialist entry treats Galileo as the reporter rather than the author.

We read the Italian rather than a summary of it. Page 319 of volume 5 of Favaro’s Edizione Nazionale ↗ has “Io qui direi quello che intesi da persona ecclesiastica costituita in eminentissimo grado, ciò é l’intenzione dello Spirito Santo essere d’insegnarci come si vadia al cielo, e non come vadia il cielo” — with the side-note Cardinal Baronio. set against it.

We also read the English. Stillman Drake’s Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo (1957) ↗ carries the sentence on p. 186, and his footnote 8 there states that “a marginal note by Galileo assigns this epigram to Cardinal Baronius (1538–1607).”
Wikipedia’s article on Baronio ↗ records the remark as his, notes that he most likely made it in conversation rather than in print, and gives his dates as 30 August 1538 to 30 June 1607.
source.excerptNote: Drake’s 1957 translation, p. 186. The line in circulation drops Galileo’s leading “That” and, more importantly, drops the clause in front of it that hands the credit to somebody else.

source.rightsNote: Two different rights questions sit on this page. Galileo’s 1615 Italian, as printed in Favaro’s 1895 Edizione Nazionale ↗, is long in the public domain. The English wording people actually quote is not: it is Stillman Drake’s, from Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo, copyright © 1957 by Stillman Drake, published by Doubleday Anchor Books. We classify by the translation shown.

author.name: Cesare Baronio
author.heading: About Cardinal Cesare Baronio
author.metaLine: 1538–1607 · Italian cardinal, Oratorian, and ecclesiastical historian
author.bio: Cesare Baronio (1538–1607) joined Philip Neri’s Oratory in Rome as a young man, was made a cardinal in 1596 and headed the Vatican Library from 1597 until his death. His Annales Ecclesiastici, a history of the Church, appeared in twelve folio volumes between 1588 and 1607. He is remembered outside church history almost entirely for a sentence he seems never to have written down — one Galileo heard him say, and quoted years later against the men who were reading astronomy out of Scripture.

He quotes it in his Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615) as something heard from "an ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree," and his marginal note names Cardinal Cesare Baronio (1538–1607). English wording: Stillman Drake, trans., Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo (Garden City, NY: Doubleday Anchor, 1957), 186.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line is quoted as Galileo’s epigram — usually as his own retort to the theologians. The clause that gives it away is the one that gets cut.

items.tag: Quoted it, did not coin it
items.why: Galileo introduces the sentence with “I would say here something that was heard from an ecclesiastic of the most eminent degree” and then sets the epigram in quotation marks. Drake’s translation, p. 186 ↗ keeps both the framing clause and the quotation marks; popular versions keep neither.
Galileo did not name him in the running text. The identification rests on his manuscript marginal note, printed as Cardinal Baronio. in the Edizione Nazionale ↗ and reported in Drake’s footnote 8.
We found no work of Baronio’s containing the sentence, and Wikipedia’s article ↗ likewise treats it as a remark made in conversation. Everything anyone knows about it comes through Galileo.

misattribution.truthLine: Galileo wrote the sentence down and made it famous. On his own marginal note ↗, the man who said it first was Cardinal Cesare Baronio.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In 1615 Galileo was not yet on trial, but the argument that would put him there was already running: if Scripture says the sun stands still over Gibeon, can the earth be the thing that moves? His long letter to Christina of Lorraine, the Grand Duchess of Tuscany, is his answer — that the Bible and nature have different jobs, and that reading one as a textbook for the other damages both.

The Baronio epigram is the letter’s sharpest sentence, and Galileo deploys it carefully. Quoting a cardinal — a Vatican librarian and the Church’s own historian — let him make the case for keeping astronomy out of theology in a voice his opponents could not easily dismiss as a mathematician’s special pleading.
detailsBody: Baronio had died in 1607, eight years before the letter was written, so he never saw the use his sentence was put to. Drake’s footnote suggests Galileo may have heard it when Baronio visited Padua with Cardinal Bellarmine in 1598, though Drake marks that as a probability rather than a fact.

The letter itself circulated in manuscript and was not the document that ended Galileo’s freedom — the 1632 Dialogue was. But its argument, and this borrowed line, are what most people mean today when they say “Galileo said” anything about faith and science.
context.pull: He was not being modest. He was borrowing a cardinal’s authority, and he said so.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists 'The intention of the Holy Ghost is to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes' in its sourced section under Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615), attributing it to an ecclesiastic glossed as '[probably Caesar Baronius]'.
Page 319 of Le opere di Galileo Galilei vol. 5 (Favaro, 1895) carries the Italian sentence and a printed marginal note reading 'Cardinal Baronio.'

Stillman Drake's Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo (1957) carries the sentence on p. 186, and footnote 8 states that a marginal note by Galileo assigns the epigram to Cardinal Baronius (1538-1607). The volume's copyright page reads 'Copyright (c) 1957 by Stillman Drake', Doubleday Anchor Books.

Wikipedia's article on Cesare Baronio gives his dates as 30 August 1538 to 30 June 1607, describes him as an Italian cardinal and ecclesiastical historian of Philip Neri's Oratory and author of the Annales Ecclesiastici (12 vols, 1588-1607), and records the heaven remark as one he probably made in conversation and that Galileo later cited.
Wikipedia's article on the Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina describes the 1615 letter and mentions Baronio in connection with the 'how the heavens go' epigram.
